source.name: sp_DynamicSearch

assumptions: The procedure is intended to return a result set, so it's converted to a FUNCTION returning TABLE
NVARCHAR types mapped to VARCHAR (PostgreSQL uses UTF-8 by default)
QUOTENAME() converted to format() with %I identifier placeholder for SQL injection protection
The calling application can handle the change from PROCEDURE to FUNCTION
The table structure is unknown, so RETURNS TABLE without explicit column definitions is used
Schema 'dbo' exists in PostgreSQL or will be created separately

reviewFlags.reason: PostgreSQL requires explicit column definitions in RETURNS TABLE for strongly-typed results. The current implementation returns an anonymous record set. Consider defining explicit columns if the table structure is known, or use RETURNS SETOF RECORD with OUT parameters.

Dynamic SQL with SELECT * may have security and performance implications. Verify that the calling application has proper validation for table and column names to prevent SQL injection. Consider whitelisting allowed tables/columns.
The function returns an untyped record set. Callers must use explicit column definitions when calling this function, e.g., SELECT * FROM sp_DynamicSearch(...) AS t(col1 type1, col2 type2, ...)
reviewFlags.codeSection: RETURN QUERY EXECUTE v_sql USING p_filter_value

compatibilityNotes.description: SQL Server procedures can return result sets implicitly. PostgreSQL functions returning TABLE must be called in SELECT statements. Calling syntax changes from EXEC sp_DynamicSearch to SELECT * FROM sp_DynamicSearch(...) AS result.
SQL Server's sp_executesql is replaced with PostgreSQL's EXECUTE...USING. Parameter binding works similarly but syntax differs.

Without explicit column definitions in RETURNS TABLE, callers must provide column list when invoking the function. This differs from SQL Server where the result set structure is determined at runtime.
PostgreSQL does not have an equivalent to SET NOCOUNT ON. Row count behavior differs between the two systems.
QUOTENAME() uses square brackets in SQL Server. PostgreSQL format() with %I uses double quotes. Both protect against SQL injection for identifiers.
